strengths: Highly practical and impactful motivation: replacing expensive external guardrail models with lightweight, single-pass probes on the serving LLM's internal states yields massive savings in VRAM and latency.

Well-designed and expressive architecture: the two-stage aggregation framework (token-level then layer-level) effectively solves the dimensionality challenge of extracting signals from the full hidden-state tensor.

Strong and comprehensive empirical results: the proposed probes (especially the MHA and scoring-attention variants) outperform logit-only baselines and match or exceed heavy standalone guard models on both safety and sentiment benchmarks.

Insightful interpretability analysis: visualizing the layer attention weights provides valuable BERTology-style insights into where different semantic and safety signals are localized across the model's depth.
weaknesses: Limited backbone diversity: the evaluation is restricted to a single model family (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct). Although the authors acknowledge this, testing on different model sizes (e.g., 8B or 70B) or other architectures (e.g., Gemma, Mistral) would greatly strengthen the generalizability claims.

Clarity on streaming generation and response moderation: the paper focuses on prompt-side moderation (evaluated with max_new_tokens=1). It is less clear how this architecture would be deployed dynamically for online/streaming response moderation without incurring substantial recurrent computation on the growing sequence.

VRAM demands during training: although inference is highly efficient, extracting, caching, and learning aggregators over the full L x T x d hidden-state tensor can be highly memory-intensive during the training phase.

strengths: Addresses a highly practical bottleneck in LLM orchestrations (the latency and VRAM cost of multi-model guardrail pipelines) with a clever, single-pass probing architecture.
Proposes a flexible and effective two-stage (token-level then layer-level) aggregation framework that successfully outperforms prior single-layer or logit-only approaches.
Includes thorough and realistic systems benchmarking (throughput, end-to-end latency, and peak GPU memory) confirming the real-world efficiency gains of the proposed probes.
Provides detailed and insightful interpretability analyses of layer-attention weights, showing distinct class-conditional depth patterns that align with classical BERTology studies.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is restricted to a single model family and size (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct), leaving the generalizability of the layer-selective probes across other popular open-source architectures (e.g., Gemma, Mistral) unverified.
Out-of-distribution generalization is somewhat limited compared to standalone models, as shown by the performance drop on ToxicChat when the probes are trained on WildGuardMix.

To train these probes without massive VRAM requirements, caching the $L \times T \times d$ hidden states is necessary, which introduces non-trivial storage and I/O bottlenecks that are not fully analyzed.

strengths: Highly practical motivation: Reusing the serving LLM's frozen activations for moderation and classification is an elegant way to reduce the latency, VRAM, and deployment complexity associated with separate 'guard' models.

Well-structured architecture: Moving away from arbitrary fixed-layer or fixed-token readouts to a structured, two-stage (token-level and layer-level) aggregation over the entire L x T x d hidden-state tensor is a principled and effective design.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper covers multiple datasets across both safety and sentiment analysis, utilizing strong baselines (standalone classifiers, APIs, and prompting-based methods) and robust out-of-distribution (OOD) transfer experiments.

Strong system and qualitative analysis: Including concrete latency/memory profiling on actual hardware (RTX 3090) validates the practical claims, while the layer attention visualizations offer interesting interpretability insights into where safety cues emerge in the network.
weaknesses: Limited backbone diversity: The empirical evaluation is restricted to Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. Testing on different model families (e.g., Gemma, Mistral) and larger scales (e.g., 70B+) would strengthen the generalization claims, especially since probe parameter counts scale with the hidden dimension $d$.

Ambiguity in dynamic streaming scenarios: It is not fully clarified how the token aggregation operates in an active autoregressive generation loop. For instance, it is unclear whether the probe is run only on the prompt, or repeated at every generated token, and how that impacts the stated system latency.

Dependency on supervised training data: Unlike prompt-based guardrails that can be easily modified on the fly, the proposed approach requires a dataset of several thousand examples to train the probes, which reduces operational flexibility when moderation policies change.

strengths: Addresses a highly practical and relevant bottleneck in production LLM deployments by replacing expensive separate guard models with lightweight, single-pass probes.

Proposes a well-designed, two-stage aggregation architecture that learns where to read information across both the sequence (tokens) and depth (layers) dimensions, rather than relying on heuristic layer or token selection.
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple distinct tasks (safety, sentiment, emotion classification) and diverse model architectures, including both dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) backbones.
Provides a thorough system-level efficiency analysis measuring end-to-end latency, throughput, and peak GPU memory, showing clear advantages over guard-then-serve baselines.
Includes a compelling interpretability analysis ('BERTology') that visualizes and discusses how different layers of the serving model encode safety and task-relevant signals.
weaknesses: The paper focuses primarily on input prompt moderation. It is less clear how the proposed probes would scale or behave computationally if applied step-by-step during autoregressive generation to moderate model outputs, as recalculating token-level and layer-level aggregation at each step could introduce cumulative latency.

Training requires access to or caching of the full three-dimensional L x T x d hidden state tensor, which can be highly VRAM-intensive and hard to scale to very long sequences or larger backbones without substantial caching/storage overhead.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and high-impact challenge in production LLM deployments: the computational and memory overhead of separate guard models for safety moderation.

The proposed two-stage aggregation template (token-level then layer-level) is conceptually simple, parameter-efficient, and elegant. The use of dimension downcasting in the MHA probe makes it computationally viable.
Excellent and thorough evaluation spanning three distinct LLM backbones (dense and mixture-of-experts), several safety datasets, and sentiment analysis benchmarks.

The 'BERTology' analysis is highly insightful; visualizing the learned attention weights across layers provides strong interpretability and solidifies the core claim that safety-relevant features are distributed rather than localized to a single layer.
weaknesses: While caching hidden states alleviates VRAM constraints during training, storing $L \times T \times d$ tensors for a large corpus remains a significant storage/I/O bottleneck that could be elaborated on.

The paper could benefit from a more direct comparison to a simple baseline that probes only the final layer's mean-pooled representation, to explicitly quantify the gain of extracting features across all intermediate layers versus just the final layer.

The deployment scenario assumes prompt classification; extending or clearly explaining how this would function for real-time streaming token generation (which requires incremental hidden state evaluation) is left somewhat abstract.

strengths: Highly Practical and Well-Motivated: The paper addresses the massive latency, memory, and orchestration overhead of deploying separate moderation models in production LLM pipelines. Reusing the serving model's forward pass is a highly practical and impactful direction.

Principled Two-Stage Aggregation Architecture: Instead of arbitrarily choosing a single layer or token (e.g., first token or final layer pooling), the paper proposes a flexible token-and-layer selective aggregator that treats the classification task as a joint representation selection problem over the full L x T x d hidden-state tensor.

Extensive and Rigorous Evaluation: The authors evaluate their probes across multiple domains (safety moderation and sentiment/emotion classification), three distinct model families (Llama-3.2, GPT-OSS, and Qwen3) spanning both dense and sparse MoE architectures, and perform out-of-distribution transfer experiments.

System-level Efficiency Benchmarking: The paper provides real-world systems measurements (latency, throughput, peak GPU memory) comparing the probes directly against popular guardrails like Llama Guard 3 and WildGuard, demonstrating substantial speedups and memory savings.

Insightful Interpretability Analysis: Section 5 provides an analytical look into the learned attention weights across layers, confirming that task-relevant information (such as toxic vs. non-toxic cues) is distributed dynamically across different depths, supporting the paper's core hypothesis.
weaknesses: Dependency on Hidden State Extraction: Training these probes requires extracting and caching large hidden-state tensors across all layers and tokens, which can incur high storage overhead and offline pipeline complexity during the training phase.

Lack of Generative Safeguard Capabilities: Unlike generative guard models (e.g., Llama Guard) which can output natural language explanations for a refusal, these probes are strictly restricted to producing classification logits and cannot natively generate contextual or explanatory rejections.

Limited Scaling Evaluation: Although the paper validates MoE backbones up to 30B total parameters, all evaluated models have around 3B active parameters. How the probe parameters and performance scale on larger dense models (e.g., 70B+ where the hidden dimension d is significantly larger) remains unaddressed.
